For cross-border work, establish legal responsibility explicitly; the selector does not decide it.

foundations.title: Professional Foundations — New South Wales
foundations.action: Identify the employer, state, service setting and any appointment required for the task.
foundations.record: Explain the professional role, consent and confidentiality limits before assessment. Consider power, racism, disability and material barriers alongside individual and family strengths. Use supervision and learning to test the effect of practice on the person, with the current AASW standards as a professional reference. Distinguish an employer complaint, a professional-association concern and a statutory regulator or tribunal route. The relevant health, disability, aged-care or child-protection body depends on the issue. A professional membership complaint is not an appeal against a state or Commonwealth funding decision.

care-support.title: Social Care and Support — New South Wales
care-support.action: Identify the scheme responsible for each need and the evidence required for its assessment.
care-support.record: Keep access eligibility, plan funding, provider availability and any client contribution separate. Consider state health, housing and community support where a need is outside a particular funded scheme. Record the person’s goals, family willingness, actual start dates and the review route for each decision. For an NDIA decision, identify whether an internal review and subsequent Administrative Review Tribunal route are available and check the decision notice’s time limits. A provider complaint to the NDIS Commission is different from a funding review. Aged-care complaints and assessment reviews use their own routes.

mca.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — New South Wales
mca.action: Support the patient’s own decision and establish the precise treatment and capacity question.
mca.record: Read the appointment and apply the person-responsible hierarchy, including eligibility and availability. Check the treatment category and whether the patient objects; do not assume a representative can override that objection. Seek the applicable NCAT or clinical/legal route where consent cannot lawfully be obtained through the ordinary hierarchy. NCAT’s Guardianship Division can deal with relevant appointments, reviews and treatment-consent applications. Explain the person’s participation and access to advice. A guardianship order must be read for its specific functions; it is not a general transfer of all decisions.

dols.title: Restrictions and Liberty — New South Wales
dols.action: Identify the practice, its purpose and whether it is a regulated restrictive practice in the actual setting.
dols.record: Check the NSW authorisation process alongside the NDIS plan, provider and reporting requirements. Verify consent or representative authority where relevant without treating it as a substitute for authorisation. Record alternatives, conditions, monitoring, review and the strategy for reducing the practice. The person should have accessible information, support to express objections and the applicable provider, NDIS Commission or legal review route. Unauthorised use may trigger incident-reporting duties. Check current rules for timing and recipients rather than waiting for routine plan review.

mha.title: Mental Health — New South Wales
mha.action: Identify the proposed route and connect the actual evidence to its criteria.
mha.record: Consider whether appropriate care is reasonably available through a less restrictive alternative. Verify the assessment, certification, notice and tribunal requirements for that status. Separate psychiatric treatment powers from consent to unrelated medical treatment and from the discharge support plan. Explain rights information, the applicable carer or designated-person arrangements, legal representation and Mental Health Review Tribunal review. Read the person’s actual documents and the current statutory time limits rather than treating every admission as a fixed period that must be completed.

safeguarding.title: Adult Safeguarding — New South Wales
safeguarding.action: Arrange a safe conversation and identify immediate danger, dependency and the adult’s desired outcomes.
safeguarding.record: Consider an ADC report where there are reasonable grounds for the relevant concern. Identify any police, NDIS Commission, aged-care or provider reporting requirement separately. Record consent and information-sharing reasoning, practical safety support and who will follow up. The ADC can explain its response and refer matters beyond its scope. Support the adult to use the relevant complaint or legal route and preserve participation where they fear retaliation. A referral is not permission to impose a placement or take over finances.

children.title: Children, Families and Transitions — New South Wales
children.action: Check the child’s age, your role and the applicable reporting threshold under the Act.
children.record: Use the current DCJ guidance and appropriate Child Protection Helpline or other reporting route. Record the concern, evidence, child’s account and report without waiting to prove the allegation. Plan family support and cultural participation, including relevant Aboriginal placement and participation requirements where engaged. Explain the role of DCJ, any court process and how the child and family can obtain support or legal advice. A voluntary support referral does not replace a mandatory report when its conditions are met. Preserve safe communication and reporter confidentiality under the applicable rules.

rights.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — New South Wales
rights.action: Identify the state or Commonwealth duty relevant to access, discrimination or the proposed intervention.
rights.record: Arrange accessible communication and culturally safe participation chosen with the person. Check the applicable information regime and lawful purpose before collection or disclosure. Explain access, correction and complaint rights, including the appropriate Information and Privacy Commission route. NSW IPC guidance distinguishes consent and other legal bases for information handling. A broad consent form does not remove all privacy obligations. A discrimination complaint, a privacy complaint and review of a service decision require different pathways.

sources.title: New South Wales Source Library
sources.action: Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.
sources.record: Record the exact source and provision used, date accessed and any unresolved question.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in New South Wales practice guide?
cards.answer: The Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW) Code of Ethics and Practice Standards provide a professional framework. AASW membership or accreditation, an employer requirement and statutory authority are different matters. Check the requirements for the actual role and state rather than presenting the professional association as the source of every legal power.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Practice should attend to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples’ self-determination, cultural safety and the effects of colonisation. Ask which community-controlled organisations or cultural supports the person wants involved. Professional values need to be connected to the state law governing the particular intervention.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the employer, state, service setting and any appointment required for the task. Explain the professional role, consent and confidentiality limits before assessment. Consider power, racism, disability and material barriers alongside individual and family strengths. Use supervision and learning to test the effect of practice on the person, with the current AASW standards as a professional reference.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Distinguish an employer complaint, a professional-association concern and a statutory regulator or tribunal route. The relevant health, disability, aged-care or child-protection body depends on the issue. A professional membership complaint is not an appeal against a state or Commonwealth funding decision.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Equating association membership, clinical experience or a job title with every statutory appointment.

flashcardDecks.title: Social Care and Support — New South Wales

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in New South Wales practice guide?
cards.answer: Disability support through the NDIS, state health and housing services, and Commonwealth aged care have separate entry and funding rules. NDIS access involves age, residence and disability or early-intervention requirements; a diagnosis alone does not establish entitlement to a particular funded support. Check current NDIA rules for the actual application or plan.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The Aged Care Act 2024 and Support at Home commenced on 1 November 2025. Do not describe the old Home Care Package arrangements as the only current system. The Commonwealth Home Support Programme has its own transition arrangements. Contributions and programme rules need a current check, including announced changes with later commencement dates.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the scheme responsible for each need and the evidence required for its assessment. Keep access eligibility, plan funding, provider availability and any client contribution separate. Consider state health, housing and community support where a need is outside a particular funded scheme. Record the person’s goals, family willingness, actual start dates and the review route for each decision.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: For an NDIA decision, identify whether an internal review and subsequent Administrative Review Tribunal route are available and check the decision notice’s time limits. A provider complaint to the NDIS Commission is different from a funding review. Aged-care complaints and assessment reviews use their own routes.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating NDIS eligibility as approval for every requested service, or using obsolete aged-care programme rules.

flashcardDecks.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — New South Wales

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in New South Wales practice guide?
cards.answer: The Guardianship Act 1987 provides important guardianship and medical-consent routes. For a patient unable to consent to relevant medical or dental treatment, identify the statutory person responsible: an authorised guardian first, then an eligible spouse or partner, unpaid carer, or close relative or friend in the prescribed order. Next of kin is not automatically the correct person.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Treatment categories and objections matter. NCAT guidance distinguishes ordinary substitute-consent situations from special treatment and situations involving an objection. An enduring guardian’s welfare functions and an attorney’s financial functions also require separate document checks.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Support the patient’s own decision and establish the precise treatment and capacity question. Read the appointment and apply the person-responsible hierarchy, including eligibility and availability. Check the treatment category and whether the patient objects; do not assume a representative can override that objection. Seek the applicable NCAT or clinical/legal route where consent cannot lawfully be obtained through the ordinary hierarchy.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: NCAT’s Guardianship Division can deal with relevant appointments, reviews and treatment-consent applications. Explain the person’s participation and access to advice. A guardianship order must be read for its specific functions; it is not a general transfer of all decisions.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating next of kin as the automatic decision-maker or ignoring an objection because a relative agrees.

flashcardDecks.title: Restrictions and Liberty — New South Wales

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in New South Wales practice guide?
cards.answer: For NDIS services, the Commonwealth behaviour-support and restrictive-practices rules operate alongside NSW authorisation requirements. A behaviour support plan, the state authorisation process and provider reporting obligations are separate parts of the framework. Lodging a plan with the NDIS Commission is not itself NSW authorisation.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: NSW DCJ publishes the Restrictive Practices Authorisation policy and procedural guide. Healthcare, aged care and mental-health settings have different rules. A person-responsible medical-consent role does not automatically authorise environmental restraint or confinement in a disability service.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the practice, its purpose and whether it is a regulated restrictive practice in the actual setting. Check the NSW authorisation process alongside the NDIS plan, provider and reporting requirements. Verify consent or representative authority where relevant without treating it as a substitute for authorisation. Record alternatives, conditions, monitoring, review and the strategy for reducing the practice.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The person should have accessible information, support to express objections and the applicable provider, NDIS Commission or legal review route. Unauthorised use may trigger incident-reporting duties. Check current rules for timing and recipients rather than waiting for routine plan review.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Equating a behaviour support plan with all state approvals, or applying disability-service rules to every hospital or care setting.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in New South Wales practice guide?
cards.answer: The Mental Health Act 2007 distinguishes mentally ill and mentally disordered persons and provides different assessment, detention and treatment routes. For the mentally ill person definition, mental illness must connect to the need for care, treatment or control to protect the person or others from serious harm. The mentally disordered route has its own serious-physical-harm test and limits.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Check the Act’s less restrictive care requirements and the exact role of authorised medical officers, the Mental Health Review Tribunal and other authorised persons. Community treatment orders and inpatient detention are different measures. A social-work qualification alone does not confer every transport or detention power.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the proposed route and connect the actual evidence to its criteria. Consider whether appropriate care is reasonably available through a less restrictive alternative. Verify the assessment, certification, notice and tribunal requirements for that status. Separate psychiatric treatment powers from consent to unrelated medical treatment and from the discharge support plan.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain rights information, the applicable carer or designated-person arrangements, legal representation and Mental Health Review Tribunal review. Read the person’s actual documents and the current statutory time limits rather than treating every admission as a fixed period that must be completed.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Confusing mentally ill and mentally disordered routes or treating a diagnosis and refusal as the whole detention test.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in New South Wales practice guide?
cards.answer: The Ageing and Disability Commissioner Act 2019 and the NSW Ageing and Disability Commission (ADC) provide a route for concerns about abuse, neglect or exploitation of older people and adults with disability. The ADC considers reports, advice, referrals and investigation within its remit, with consent and statutory exceptions relevant to investigation.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Concerns about an NDIS provider, an aged-care service, a health service, crime or family violence may require a different or additional route. Identify the setting and relationship; one report to the ADC does not necessarily discharge another organisation’s incident-reporting duties.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Arrange a safe conversation and identify immediate danger, dependency and the adult’s desired outcomes. Consider an ADC report where there are reasonable grounds for the relevant concern. Identify any police, NDIS Commission, aged-care or provider reporting requirement separately. Record consent and information-sharing reasoning, practical safety support and who will follow up.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The ADC can explain its response and refer matters beyond its scope. Support the adult to use the relevant complaint or legal route and preserve participation where they fear retaliation. A referral is not permission to impose a placement or take over finances.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Assuming that every adult-safety concern belongs to one agency or that reporting creates substitute decision-making powers.

flashcardDecks.title: Children, Families and Transitions — New South Wales

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in New South Wales practice guide?
cards.answer: The Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998 provides the child-protection framework. Mandatory-reporting obligations depend on the professional role and circumstances, including reasonable grounds to suspect a child is at risk of significant harm. The statutory mandatory duty for a child and the ability to report concerns about a young person must be distinguished.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: DCJ’s Mandatory Reporter Guide supports decisions about the response but does not replace the Act or immediate safety action. Child-protection reporting, police reporting and an organisation’s incident or reportable-conduct procedures can be separate duties.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Check the child’s age, your role and the applicable reporting threshold under the Act. Use the current DCJ guidance and appropriate Child Protection Helpline or other reporting route. Record the concern, evidence, child’s account and report without waiting to prove the allegation. Plan family support and cultural participation, including relevant Aboriginal placement and participation requirements where engaged.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain the role of DCJ, any court process and how the child and family can obtain support or legal advice. A voluntary support referral does not replace a mandatory report when its conditions are met. Preserve safe communication and reporter confidentiality under the applicable rules.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating a support referral or an internal incident entry as the required child-protection report.

flashcardDecks.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — New South Wales

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in New South Wales practice guide?
cards.answer: The Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 and relevant Commonwealth discrimination laws form part of the NSW rights map. For records, distinguish the Privacy and Personal Information Protection Act 1998 from the Health Records and Information Privacy Act 2002 (HRIP), as well as any Commonwealth privacy obligations applying to the organisation.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The HRIP health-privacy principles concern collection, storage, access, use and disclosure within their statutory scope. Identify whether the organisation is a public agency, health-service provider or another covered entity. A service’s privacy policy should explain its duties, not be treated as a separate permission to disregard them.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the state or Commonwealth duty relevant to access, discrimination or the proposed intervention. Arrange accessible communication and culturally safe participation chosen with the person. Check the applicable information regime and lawful purpose before collection or disclosure. Explain access, correction and complaint rights, including the appropriate Information and Privacy Commission route.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: NSW IPC guidance distinguishes consent and other legal bases for information handling. A broad consent form does not remove all privacy obligations. A discrimination complaint, a privacy complaint and review of a service decision require different pathways.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Assuming that working with the same person creates unrestricted authority to share health records.

Continuing professional development: learning, reflection and evidence of improvement.
Agreement to a specific action; check the applicable requirements for information, voluntariness and ability to consent.

A reasoned account connecting evidence and possible explanations to a plan.
Relationships that may offer support; availability, safety and willingness need assessment.
Planned change between services or life stages, with continuity and named responsibilities.
An agreed response if risks increase or the preferred plan cannot operate.
A planned check of outcomes, changing circumstances and whether actions remain appropriate.
An option that can achieve the purpose with less interference in rights and freedom.

theoryLenses.title: Ecological Systems Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Person, family, housing, community, services, poverty, policy, culture, and environment.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be shaped by pressures around the person, not only by individual behaviour or choice.
test: What changed in the environment before the concern escalated?
Which systems are supporting the person, and which are adding pressure?
Would risk reduce if housing, income, access, care, or community support changed?

theoryLenses.title: Strengths-Based Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Capabilities, identity, relationships, community, culture, hope, and what is already working.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may have protective strategies or relationships that are hidden by a risk-heavy professional account.
test: What has helped the person survive or cope so far?
Who does the person trust, and what role could they safely play?
Which strengths are real evidence, and which are optimistic assumptions?

theoryLenses.title: Trauma-Informed Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, shame, threat responses, and control.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Behaviour that looks like refusal, avoidance, anger, or disengagement may be a survival response to trauma, coercion, loss, or fear.
test: What might feel unsafe or controlling from the person's perspective?
What helps the person feel more choice and predictability?
How can we avoid repeating patterns of powerlessness?

theoryLenses.title: Attachment Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Trust, separation, dependency, rejection, fear, care-seeking, and relationship patterns.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Responses to professionals or carers may reflect previous experiences of care, loss, abandonment, or unsafe relationships.
test: How does the person respond when support increases, reduces, or changes?
Are there patterns of clinging, pushing away, testing, mistrust, or fear?
What relationship approach is consistent, boundaried, and safe?

theoryLenses.title: Systems and Family Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Roles, rules, communication, repeated patterns, conflict, care dynamics, and network effects.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The concern may be maintained by relationship patterns, family roles, service responses, or network conflict.
test: Who gains or loses if the current pattern changes?
What role has each person been placed in or taken on?
How do professional responses affect the family or network pattern?

theoryLenses.title: Anti-Oppressive and Anti-Discriminatory Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Power, oppression, racism, disability, class, gender, sexuality, culture, age, stigma, and access.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be intensified by structural inequality, professional power, discrimination, or inaccessible services.
test: What barriers has the person faced before we became involved?
Whose account is being treated as most credible, and why?
What reasonable adjustments, cultural humility, or advocacy are needed?

theoryLenses.title: Crisis Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Immediate stress, narrowed options, temporary disequilibrium, coping capacity, and stabilisation.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person or family may be temporarily overwhelmed and need stabilisation before longer-term planning is realistic.
test: What immediate event or loss has exceeded usual coping?
What needs to happen in the next 24 to 72 hours?
What can wait until safety, sleep, food, medication, or support is more stable?

theoryLenses.title: Life Course Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Transitions, cumulative disadvantage, ageing, identity, loss, timing, and turning points.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Current risk or distress may connect to earlier life events, cumulative exclusion, transition, bereavement, or changing identity.
test: What transitions or losses are happening now?
How has cumulative disadvantage shaped options and trust?
What strengths, relationships, or identities from earlier life still matter?

theoryLenses.title: Task-Centred Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Specific problems, agreed goals, small steps, roles, review, and measurable change.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may benefit from breaking an overwhelming issue into concrete, negotiated tasks with clear review.
test: What problem does the person most want to work on first?
What is the smallest useful next step?
Who will do what, by when, and how will we know it helped?

hypothesisSignals.label: Self-neglect, hoarding, home conditions, or repeated crisis presentations.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Think about trauma, executive functioning, environment, identity, isolation, loss, and safeguarding thresholds.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person appears to refuse support, miss visits, or disengage.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Avoid jumping straight to non-compliance. Consider trust, trauma, power, communication, and whether the offer fits the person.

hypothesisSignals.label: Family conflict, carer strain, coercion, or unclear roles are present.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Map roles, power, risk, protective factors, and what happens when professionals intervene.

hypothesisSignals.label: Risk has escalated quickly or a crisis is dominating the assessment.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Separate immediate stabilisation from longer-term formulation and legal route decisions.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is a transition: adolescence to adulthood, hospital discharge, bereavement, moving home, or ageing.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Transitions can disrupt identity, support, eligibility, relationships, and coping.

hypothesisSignals.label: Discrimination, poverty, inaccessible services, stigma, or cultural misunderstanding may be relevant.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Test whether systems are creating or worsening the difficulty.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person or carer feels overwhelmed and cannot see a way forward.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Consider crisis, small steps, stabilisation, advocacy, and practical environmental change.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is mistrust of professionals, fear of services, or repeated complaints.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Explore previous experiences, power, communication, consistency, and whether the person has reason to feel unsafe.

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Safety
childPracticeModels.use: Child protection mapping, danger statements, safety goals, family network work, scaling, and safety planning.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What are we worried about, what is working well, and what needs to happen for the child to be safe enough?
test: Can worries be written in plain language that the family understands?
What existing safety has been demonstrated, not just promised?
Who is in the family network and what role can they safely take?

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Wellbeing, Success, and Belonging
childPracticeModels.use: Family support, children in care, permanency, reunification, stability, identity, and belonging work.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What would wellbeing, safety, permanence, connection, and belonging look like from the child's perspective?
test: What does the child say or show about where they feel safe and connected?
What would meaningful stability look like in daily life?
How are family relationships, identity, culture, and belonging being protected?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Whole-family child protection where parental domestic abuse, mental health, substance misuse, trauma, or adult needs affect child safety.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety may improve when adult needs and risks are addressed alongside direct work with the child and family network.
test: Which adult needs are directly affecting child safety or care?
Is the plan joined up across children's and adults' services?
Are adult-focused interventions linked to measurable child safety outcomes?

childPracticeModels.title: Contextual Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Extra-familial harm, exploitation, peer group risk, school, neighbourhood, online spaces, and adolescent safeguarding.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Harm may be located outside the home, in peer, school, community, or online contexts that parents cannot control alone.
test: Where is harm happening: home, school, peer group, community, online, or transport?
Which context needs intervention, not only which child or parent?
Who has power or influence in that context?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Group Conferencing
childPracticeModels.use: Family-led planning, kinship care, safety planning, pre-proceedings, reunification, and support network building.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The wider family network may hold safe, practical solutions that have not yet been fully mapped or invited in.
test: Who does the child identify as family or trusted network?
What information does the family need before private planning?
How will the plan be checked for safety, clarity, and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Systemic Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Family patterns, repeated cycles, communication, roles, meaning, conflict, and relationship-based formulation.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The concern may be maintained by family patterns, relationship roles, service responses, or repeated cycles.
test: What pattern repeats, and what keeps it going?
How does each person make sense of the problem?
What would change if one part of the system responded differently?

childPracticeModels.title: Motivational Interviewing
childPracticeModels.use: Ambivalence, parental engagement, adolescent risk, substance use, resistance, and behaviour change conversations.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The parent or young person may be caught between reasons to change and reasons to keep things as they are.
test: What does the person want to be different?
What are their reasons for change and reasons against change?
Are we arguing for change so hard that the person argues against it?

childPracticeModels.title: Solution-Focused Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Goal-setting, exceptions, scaling, strengths, future-focused planning, and building on small signs of progress.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Small exceptions or signs of safety may reveal what can be repeated, strengthened, and built into the plan.
test: When is the problem slightly less serious?
What would one point higher on the safety scale look like?
What has the family already done that helped, even briefly?

childPracticeModels.title: PACE and DDP-Informed Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Children affected by trauma, attachment disruption, care experience, shame, mistrust, and blocked trust.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The child may need relational safety through playfulness, acceptance, curiosity, and empathy before they can reflect or change.
test: How does the child's behaviour make sense as communication or protection?
How can adults stay curious without shaming or escalating?
What helps the child experience safety in the relationship?

childPracticeModels.title: Safe and Together
childPracticeModels.use: Domestic abuse-informed child welfare, perpetrator pattern mapping, protective parent strengths, and child impact.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety work should focus on the perpetrator's pattern of behaviour and avoid blaming the non-abusive parent for the abuse.
test: What is the perpetrator's pattern and impact on the child?
What has the protective parent done to promote safety?
Does the plan increase accountability for the person causing harm?

childPracticeModels.title: Graded Care Profile 2
childPracticeModels.use: Neglect assessment, evidence-based care mapping, physical care, safety, love and esteem, and developmental care.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The quality of care may need structured, observable mapping rather than vague descriptions of neglect.
test: Which care domains are strong, inconsistent, or harmful?
What evidence has been observed rather than assumed?
Is change measurable across time and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Restorative Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Repair, accountability, family meetings, school relationships, conflict, shame, and shared problem-solving.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Progress may come through relationship repair, accountability, and shared planning rather than only professional direction.
test: Who has been affected and what do they need?
What repair or accountability is realistic and safe?
How will the meeting avoid blame and keep the child central?

childModelSignals.label: Child protection concerns, safety planning, or danger statements are needed.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs clear worries, existing safety, safety goals, family network planning, and review.

childModelSignals.label: Neglect, home conditions, missed health needs, or inconsistent care are central.
childModelSignals.detail: The assessment needs observable evidence, care domains, impact on the child, and change over time.

childModelSignals.label: Domestic abuse is affecting the child or family safety.
childModelSignals.detail: The plan needs perpetrator pattern analysis, protective parent strengths, child impact, and safe information sharing.

childModelSignals.label: Exploitation, adolescent risk, peer harm, school risk, or online/community harm is present.
childModelSignals.detail: Risk may sit outside the home and require contextual mapping beyond parent-focused plans.

childModelSignals.label: The child is in care, on the edge of care, returning home, or permanence is uncertain.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs belonging, stability, identity, relationships, family network options, and safe permanence planning.

childModelSignals.label: Trauma, attachment disruption, mistrust, shame, or relational conflict is central.
childModelSignals.detail: The child may need relational safety and adults who can stay curious, calm, boundaried, and empathic.

childModelSignals.label: There may be wider family or trusted network members who could help.
childModelSignals.detail: The network may hold safe options for care, practical support, supervision, or belonging.

childModelSignals.label: A parent or young person feels ambivalent, defensive, stuck, or hard to engage.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs careful engagement, change talk, respect for autonomy, and clarity about non-negotiable safety.

childModelSignals.label: There has been conflict, harm, school exclusion, relationship breakdown, or a need for repair.
childModelSignals.detail: The work may need accountability, safe dialogue, relationship repair, and a shared plan.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Professional Foundations — New South Wales
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A practitioner is asked to sign a statutory assessment because they hold an AASW credential, without checking the specific appointment requirements.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Read the law and service procedure governing that assessment. Confirm qualifications, appointment and scope before signing. Bring any gap to the responsible manager and arrange an authorised practitioner while continuing work that is within your role.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Social Care and Support — New South Wales
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A person is told that their NDIS plan should pay for every need after a hospital admission, including treatment and unsuitable housing.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Map the actual support sought and the responsibility of each system. Obtain the relevant decisions and coordinate health, housing and disability support. Record unmet needs and interim arrangements rather than presenting an unfunded referral as a completed plan.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — New South Wales
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A daughter who manages bills offers consent for a procedure, while the patient objects and an appointed guardian has a medical-consent function.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check the patient’s decision-making ability and objection, then the guardian’s actual authority and the treatment category. The daughter’s financial help does not settle the consent route. Obtain the appropriate specialist or NCAT advice rather than collecting whichever signature is easiest.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Restrictions and Liberty — New South Wales
scenarioWorkouts.summary: An NDIS provider locks kitchen cupboards and says the uploaded behaviour plan is all the permission it needs.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Identify the restriction’s purpose and effect, examine the NSW authorisation requirements and check the person’s participation. Consider less restrictive access and support. Resolve missing approvals and any incident duties with the responsible practitioners; an uploaded plan does not resolve them.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Mental Health — New South Wales
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A person declines admission but accepts a crisis-team visit and support from a friend. Staff describe the refusal as sufficient reason for detention.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Assess the harm evidence and whether the offered alternative is suitable and available. Ask the authorised clinician to apply the relevant criteria and record the reasoning. The refusal is one fact to understand, not a complete statutory assessment.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Adult Safeguarding — New South Wales
scenarioWorkouts.summary: An older person reports that a relative takes their money, while a provider separately fails to deliver agreed meals.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Map the financial exploitation and the service failure as distinct concerns. Arrange immediate food access and safe contact, consider ADC and any police response, and pursue the provider or regulator pathway for missed care. Check who has accepted each action.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Children, Families and Transitions — New South Wales
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A worker hears a child describe violence at home and is told that a referral to a family-support charity is sufficient.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Assess immediate safety and the significant-harm concern, check the reporting duty and use the appropriate DCJ or police route. Family support may be valuable alongside that action, but it cannot be used to avoid an applicable statutory report.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — New South Wales
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A provider proposes sending a complete health record to a housing worker because both organisations support the same client.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Clarify the housing decision, the relevant information and the applicable privacy framework. Seek or identify the appropriate legal basis, respect confidentiality limits and record what is shared. The shared client does not make unrestricted file exchange necessary.

printableTemplates.title: Professional Foundations
printableTemplates.summary: Explain your professional role, distinguish an ethical concern from a statutory power, and turn a formulation into an accountable plan.
printableTemplates.body:
Professional Foundations
New South Wales practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW) Code of Ethics and Practice Standards provide a professional framework. AASW membership or accreditation, an employer requirement and statutory authority are different matters. Check the requirements for the actual role and state rather than presenting the professional association as the source of every legal power.

Practice should attend to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples’ self-determination, cultural safety and the effects of colonisation. Ask which community-controlled organisations or cultural supports the person wants involved. Professional values need to be connected to the state law governing the particular intervention.

Local pathway:
Identify the employer, state, service setting and any appointment required for the task.
Explain the professional role, consent and confidentiality limits before assessment.
Consider power, racism, disability and material barriers alongside individual and family strengths.
Use supervision and learning to test the effect of practice on the person, with the current AASW standards as a professional reference.

Recording prompts:
1. Your role and the legal or professional framework
Notes:

2. The person’s outcomes and communication preferences
Notes:

3. Evidence, competing explanations and missing perspectives
Notes:

4. Power, boundaries and any conflict of interest
Notes:

5. Agreed action, supervision, feedback and review
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Distinguish an employer complaint, a professional-association concern and a statutory regulator or tribunal route. The relevant health, disability, aged-care or child-protection body depends on the issue. A professional membership complaint is not an appeal against a state or Commonwealth funding decision.

Sources:
https://www.aasw.asn.au/about-aasw/ethics-standards/code-of-ethics/

printableTemplates.title: Social Care and Support
printableTemplates.summary: Map assessment, eligibility, funding and delivery separately; include family support without assuming it; explain the local route for challenging a decision.
printableTemplates.body:
Social Care and Support
New South Wales practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Disability support through the NDIS, state health and housing services, and Commonwealth aged care have separate entry and funding rules. NDIS access involves age, residence and disability or early-intervention requirements; a diagnosis alone does not establish entitlement to a particular funded support. Check current NDIA rules for the actual application or plan.

The Aged Care Act 2024 and Support at Home commenced on 1 November 2025. Do not describe the old Home Care Package arrangements as the only current system. The Commonwealth Home Support Programme has its own transition arrangements. Contributions and programme rules need a current check, including announced changes with later commencement dates.

Local pathway:
Identify the scheme responsible for each need and the evidence required for its assessment.
Keep access eligibility, plan funding, provider availability and any client contribution separate.
Consider state health, housing and community support where a need is outside a particular funded scheme.
Record the person’s goals, family willingness, actual start dates and the review route for each decision.

Recording prompts:
1. Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
Notes:

2. The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
Notes:

3. Carer willingness and separately identified needs
Notes:

4. Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
Notes:

5. Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
For an NDIA decision, identify whether an internal review and subsequent Administrative Review Tribunal route are available and check the decision notice’s time limits. A provider complaint to the NDIS Commission is different from a funding review. Aged-care complaints and assessment reviews use their own routes.

Sources:
https://ndis.gov.au/applying/application-process/what-access-request-form
https://ndis.gov.au/ndis-laws/getting-ndis-back-track/summary-legislation-changes
https://www.health.gov.au/our-work/aged-care-act/resources/providers
https://www.health.gov.au/our-work/chsp/reforms

printableTemplates.title: Decision-Making and Capacity
printableTemplates.summary: Identify the precise decision, provide practical decision support, apply the local capacity or consent framework and verify a representative’s authority.
printableTemplates.body:
Decision-Making and Capacity
New South Wales practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Guardianship Act 1987 provides important guardianship and medical-consent routes. For a patient unable to consent to relevant medical or dental treatment, identify the statutory person responsible: an authorised guardian first, then an eligible spouse or partner, unpaid carer, or close relative or friend in the prescribed order. Next of kin is not automatically the correct person.

Treatment categories and objections matter. NCAT guidance distinguishes ordinary substitute-consent situations from special treatment and situations involving an objection. An enduring guardian’s welfare functions and an attorney’s financial functions also require separate document checks.

Local pathway:
Support the patient’s own decision and establish the precise treatment and capacity question.
Read the appointment and apply the person-responsible hierarchy, including eligibility and availability.
Check the treatment category and whether the patient objects; do not assume a representative can override that objection.
Seek the applicable NCAT or clinical/legal route where consent cannot lawfully be obtained through the ordinary hierarchy.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, options and time at which it is needed
Notes:

2. Communication support and observed responses
Notes:

3. Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
Notes:

4. Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
Notes:

5. Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action
Notes:

Challenge and review:
NCAT’s Guardianship Division can deal with relevant appointments, reviews and treatment-consent applications. Explain the person’s participation and access to advice. A guardianship order must be read for its specific functions; it is not a general transfer of all decisions.

Sources:
https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/publications-and-resources/fact-sheets/person-responsible-fact-sheet.html
https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/view/html/inforce/current/act-1987-257
https://ncat.nsw.gov.au/case-types/guardianship.html

printableTemplates.title: Restrictions and Liberty
printableTemplates.summary: Describe actual restrictions, identify the setting-specific legal authority, test alternatives and make representation and review practical.
printableTemplates.body:
Restrictions and Liberty
New South Wales practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
For NDIS services, the Commonwealth behaviour-support and restrictive-practices rules operate alongside NSW authorisation requirements. A behaviour support plan, the state authorisation process and provider reporting obligations are separate parts of the framework. Lodging a plan with the NDIS Commission is not itself NSW authorisation.

NSW DCJ publishes the Restrictive Practices Authorisation policy and procedural guide. Healthcare, aged care and mental-health settings have different rules. A person-responsible medical-consent role does not automatically authorise environmental restraint or confinement in a disability service.

Local pathway:
Identify the practice, its purpose and whether it is a regulated restrictive practice in the actual setting.
Check the NSW authorisation process alongside the NDIS plan, provider and reporting requirements.
Verify consent or representative authority where relevant without treating it as a substitute for authorisation.
Record alternatives, conditions, monitoring, review and the strategy for reducing the practice.

Recording prompts:
1. Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
Notes:

2. The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
Notes:

3. Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
Notes:

4. Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
Notes:

5. Representation, review date, expiry and challenge
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The person should have accessible information, support to express objections and the applicable provider, NDIS Commission or legal review route. Unauthorised use may trigger incident-reporting duties. Check current rules for timing and recipients rather than waiting for routine plan review.

Sources:
https://dcj.nsw.gov.au/service-providers/deliver-disability-services/restrictive-practices-authorisation-portal/policy.html
https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au/rules-and-standards/behaviour-support-and-restrictive-practices/rules-implementing-providers

printableTemplates.title: Mental Health
printableTemplates.summary: Distinguish voluntary care, compulsory assessment, detention and treatment; connect the local criteria to evidence and explain the person’s review rights.
printableTemplates.body:
Mental Health
New South Wales practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Mental Health Act 2007 distinguishes mentally ill and mentally disordered persons and provides different assessment, detention and treatment routes. For the mentally ill person definition, mental illness must connect to the need for care, treatment or control to protect the person or others from serious harm. The mentally disordered route has its own serious-physical-harm test and limits.

Check the Act’s less restrictive care requirements and the exact role of authorised medical officers, the Mental Health Review Tribunal and other authorised persons. Community treatment orders and inpatient detention are different measures. A social-work qualification alone does not confer every transport or detention power.

Local pathway:
Identify the proposed route and connect the actual evidence to its criteria.
Consider whether appropriate care is reasonably available through a less restrictive alternative.
Verify the assessment, certification, notice and tribunal requirements for that status.
Separate psychiatric treatment powers from consent to unrelated medical treatment and from the discharge support plan.

Recording prompts:
1. Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
Notes:

2. The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
Notes:

3. Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
Notes:

4. Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
Notes:

5. Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain rights information, the applicable carer or designated-person arrangements, legal representation and Mental Health Review Tribunal review. Read the person’s actual documents and the current statutory time limits rather than treating every admission as a fixed period that must be completed.

Sources:
https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/view/html/inforce/current/act-2007-008
https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/view/pdf/inforce/current/act-2007-008

printableTemplates.title: Adult Safeguarding
printableTemplates.summary: Recognise abuse, neglect and coercion; choose the correct local reporting route; connect immediate protection to the adult’s wishes and continuing support.
printableTemplates.body:
Adult Safeguarding
New South Wales practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Ageing and Disability Commissioner Act 2019 and the NSW Ageing and Disability Commission (ADC) provide a route for concerns about abuse, neglect or exploitation of older people and adults with disability. The ADC considers reports, advice, referrals and investigation within its remit, with consent and statutory exceptions relevant to investigation.

Concerns about an NDIS provider, an aged-care service, a health service, crime or family violence may require a different or additional route. Identify the setting and relationship; one report to the ADC does not necessarily discharge another organisation’s incident-reporting duties.

Local pathway:
Arrange a safe conversation and identify immediate danger, dependency and the adult’s desired outcomes.
Consider an ADC report where there are reasonable grounds for the relevant concern.
Identify any police, NDIS Commission, aged-care or provider reporting requirement separately.
Record consent and information-sharing reasoning, practical safety support and who will follow up.

Recording prompts:
1. Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
Notes:

2. Immediate safety and a safe communication method
Notes:

3. The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
Notes:

4. Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
Notes:

5. Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The ADC can explain its response and refer matters beyond its scope. Support the adult to use the relevant complaint or legal route and preserve participation where they fear retaliation. A referral is not permission to impose a placement or take over finances.

Sources:
https://ageingdisabilitycommission.nsw.gov.au/about-us/reporting/our-response-to-reports.html
https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/view/html/inforce/current/act-2019-007

printableTemplates.title: Children, Families and Transitions
printableTemplates.summary: Separate family support from protection powers, apply the local reporting duty, involve the child and coordinate education, health and transition planning.
printableTemplates.body:
Children, Families and Transitions
New South Wales practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Children and Young Persons (Care and Protection) Act 1998 provides the child-protection framework. Mandatory-reporting obligations depend on the professional role and circumstances, including reasonable grounds to suspect a child is at risk of significant harm. The statutory mandatory duty for a child and the ability to report concerns about a young person must be distinguished.

DCJ’s Mandatory Reporter Guide supports decisions about the response but does not replace the Act or immediate safety action. Child-protection reporting, police reporting and an organisation’s incident or reportable-conduct procedures can be separate duties.

Local pathway:
Check the child’s age, your role and the applicable reporting threshold under the Act.
Use the current DCJ guidance and appropriate Child Protection Helpline or other reporting route.
Record the concern, evidence, child’s account and report without waiting to prove the allegation.
Plan family support and cultural participation, including relevant Aboriginal placement and participation requirements where engaged.

Recording prompts:
1. Child’s account, communication and daily-life evidence
Notes:

2. Harm, strengths, needs and alternative explanations
Notes:

3. Reporting duty, recipient and action taken
Notes:

4. Family participation, culture and legal authority
Notes:

5. Named plan, education/health links and transition dates
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain the role of DCJ, any court process and how the child and family can obtain support or legal advice. A voluntary support referral does not replace a mandatory report when its conditions are met. Preserve safe communication and reporter confidentiality under the applicable rules.

Sources:
https://dcj.nsw.gov.au/children-and-families/protecting-our-kids/mandatory-reporters/who-are-mandatory-reporters.html
https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/view/html/inforce/current/act-1998-157

printableTemplates.title: Rights, Culture and Recording
printableTemplates.summary: Connect rights to an actual service decision, distinguish privacy from absolute secrecy and write a record that makes reasons and disagreement visible.
printableTemplates.body:
Rights, Culture and Recording
New South Wales practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 and relevant Commonwealth discrimination laws form part of the NSW rights map. For records, distinguish the Privacy and Personal Information Protection Act 1998 from the Health Records and Information Privacy Act 2002 (HRIP), as well as any Commonwealth privacy obligations applying to the organisation.

The HRIP health-privacy principles concern collection, storage, access, use and disclosure within their statutory scope. Identify whether the organisation is a public agency, health-service provider or another covered entity. A service’s privacy policy should explain its duties, not be treated as a separate permission to disregard them.

Local pathway:
Identify the state or Commonwealth duty relevant to access, discrimination or the proposed intervention.
Arrange accessible communication and culturally safe participation chosen with the person.
Check the applicable information regime and lawful purpose before collection or disclosure.
Explain access, correction and complaint rights, including the appropriate Information and Privacy Commission route.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, affected rights and responsible organisation
Notes:

2. Accessibility, culture and participation arrangements
Notes:

3. Disclosure purpose, legal basis, recipient and limits
Notes:

4. Evidence, alternatives, reasons and disagreement
Notes:

5. Access, correction, complaints and review route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
NSW IPC guidance distinguishes consent and other legal bases for information handling. A broad consent form does not remove all privacy obligations. A discrimination complaint, a privacy complaint and review of a service decision require different pathways.

Sources:
https://www.ipc.nsw.gov.au/resources/fact-sheet-health-privacy-principles-hpps
https://www.ipc.nsw.gov.au/privacy/nsw-privacy-laws/hrip
https://legislation.nsw.gov.au/view/html/inforce/current/act-1977-048
